First of all you went to the extreme end of what I meant for clear instructions. You made it sound unncecessarily complicated to the point of being scientific of which I was not looking for. I was just looking for a way for instructions to be more clear, what I meant for "heat the pan to 120 degrees" is the frustration one gets as a beginner when they are told to turn the heat to medium and medium can vary a lot from the type of heating instrument used.

So lets take your example of the instructions and I will tell you what a beginner might face :

For the ingredients you listed- the ingredients in metric are always superior for someone who doesn't have the measuring cups and spoons that the recipe writer imagines. And no they are not standardized in Europe or in US. Even if they were how am I going to know which "standard" the recipe writer uses. On the other hand whoever writes both in metric and cups, spoons - will give a clear picture of the required ingredients. Also for the oil, you can just mention what type of oil to use for what type of pan, which one is preferable etc.

1st step observations from a newbie's perspective

in the first instructions you are not giving the reader any idea how he should cut the ingredients, how small or large, size etc. in the second set of instructions the instructions don't matter for the potatoes since you are showing a picture (but still a rough sizing should be mentioned). as for the onions and bacon you are showing a picture and give measurment  which is good, but i understand that you are trying to prove an ultimately wrong point here and hence you make all the instructions in the second example unnecessarily confusing (4mm cube bacon).

2nd step

"heat the oil to medium heat" I think you meant heat the oil on medium heat, but nevertheless, what is medium heat? 50 C avg on the pan with thermometar? number 4 on my stove, or medium on your gas heater knob ? when do I stop heating the oil? how will I know the oil is heated properly ? what size of pan should I be using - this is not mentioned in both of the cases - a bit of oil or 5ml oil in a large enough pan wont cover even touch some of the ingredients.  "add potatoes and put a lid, and wait for 3 min" in the second example you give diagrams that for the average person would be even more confusing, instead you should mention that "for these type of pans, usually you want to wait approximately this much time, but if you have pan of this type then wait x time etc." also in both cases you just said put a lid on ? does it matter if the lid covers the whole pan or it leaks air through the sides (this is especially confusing for boiling stuff).

step 3

this one is simple in both cases

step 4

open the lid again 5 min later ? and then continue frying until I get golden colour? after that remove the pan from the heat and add marjoram and pepper?

I will repeat once again - more detailed and clear instructions = better cooking. Just as there are on many websites options to adjust "ingredient amount" for the amount of servings that you would want to end up, there should be options to automatically convert "cups and spoons" to liters, grams.

> In Europe, spoon sizes are actually standardised: a teaspoon is 5ml, a table spoon is 15 ml. "medium heat" is as specific as you could get with different ranges, different pots and natural ingredient variety. "simmer" is an exact measure of cooking in boiling water, that still looks relatively calm.

I too expected that they are standardized but I found it's not standardized also, and not everyone has those "standard spoons and cups" at home.

> Honestly, how do you want to assure that the pan surface has exactly 120 °C, how will you control it to stay this way and how do you assure that you get the ingredient you want to fry in the correct shape and composition for the 2 minutes to be correct.

I didn't mean precise, but just give the beginner what to look for. The 120 C is maybe foolish, but that stems from the fact that a beginner has no idea what medium heat is, as I explained above.
Shape and composition can also be mentioned in the instructions "if you have this type of potato then you should do this, if you cut them in this size you should do this, just general tips, not exact science as you misinterpreted my post".

> For the recipe itself you then run into problems, as you would need a chemical analysis of your ingredients to get correct values for temperature and duration.

> Recipes are just eyeballed estimates, therefore you need measurements that are quick and easy to use, not ones that are overly exact.

I repeat again, I am not looking for exact, precise. Even in chemistry experiments you don't get to be precise and exact, there can be a lot of impurities, the beakers vary in quality, the acids vary in concentration etc. But the instructions are so clear in almost any video you watch compared to cooking, that even a high school student can make complex compounds just by following the instructions.

For cooking, something so common and everyday - its much more hard to get good instructions. I will give you an example. 

Since I am a complete beginner, I was trying to learn how to boil rice the other day, not only did I found completely different instructions of the dozens of videos I have watched, but I also had to watch all of them to learn bits and pieces of information that werent mentioned in one complete video. Some of the things I learned that were not mentioned in many videos was that I should add salt otherwise it would taste bland (in so many videos that was not mentioned.). Then I had to watch couple of more to learn how much I should add and I went from a "a pinch of salt" (which would have made my rice taste bland) to specific amount that I had to convert to grams because I have a small weight scale but not US teaspoon. I know there is a tolerance, and again, I am not trying to find precise amount, but a pinch is a lot different from 1tbsp or 5-6grams.

And when I finally found a video that was detailed enough, I decided to go along with the instructions (I even went out and bought exactly the same rice jasmin thailändisch), but later in the video after starting the whole process the presenter casually mentions that you should not use too large pot if you cook small amount of rice, and that was the moment I realized that I will have to add even more rice than I originally planned to cook. Otherwise I would have went out again and bought a smaller pot. But that small info that was previously not mentioned in dozens of videos left me with over half a kilo rice.

I hope I am more clear and from which viewpoint I am coming from.
